questions.question: What must an identity element do to every element of the set?
options: Make the operation commutative.
Send it to zero.
Swap it with its inverse.
Leave it unchanged on both sides.
questions.explanation: An identity $e$ for $\star$ satisfies $e\star a=a$ and $a\star e=a$ for every $a$. It is neutral on both sides.
questions.source_support: Definition: $a\star e=e\star a=a$ for all $a\in A$.

questions.question: Why is “on both sides” included for an identity element?
options: Because the identity must be outside the set.
A one-sided neutral element may not be neutral when placed on the other side.
Because every operation is commutative.
Because binary operations always have two different identities.
questions.explanation: Without commutativity, $a\star e=a$ does not imply $e\star a=a$. A two-sided identity must satisfy both equations explicitly.

questions.question: If an identity element exists for a binary operation, how many can there be?
options: Infinitely many whenever the set is nonempty.
At most one.
Exactly two.
One for each element of the set.
questions.explanation: If $e$ and $f$ are identities, then $e\star f=f$ because $e$ is a left identity, while $e\star f=e$ because $f$ is a right identity. Thus $e=f$.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: if an identity element exists, it is unique.

questions.question: Why is the identity element operation-dependent?
options: An identity element is chosen only by notation.
The same set cannot carry two operations.
Every operation has identity $0$.
$0$ for addition, $1$ for multiplication.
questions.explanation: Neutrality depends on the operation: $a+0=0+a=a$, while $a\cdot1=1\cdot a=a$. Hence the same set can have different identities for different operations.
questions.source_support: Examples: $0$ is the identity for addition; $1$ is the identity for multiplication.

questions.question: What is the difference between an identity element and an absorbing element?
options: Identity leaves elements unchanged; absorbing collapses them.
An absorbing element must be outside the set.
An identity changes every element into its inverse.
They are the same concept in every operation.
questions.explanation: An identity satisfies $e\star a=a$, whereas an absorbing element $z$ satisfies $z\star a=z$. One preserves the other input; the other collapses it.

questions.question: Why does the uniqueness proof for identity elements start by comparing two candidates $e$ and $f$?

questions.explanation: Identity is only one group axiom. For example, nonnegative integers under addition form a monoid with identity $0$, but positive elements have no additive inverse inside the set.

questions.question: On the positive real numbers under addition, why is there no identity element?

The additive identity would be $0$, but $0$ is not positive.
The identity would be $1$, but $1$ is positive.
Every positive number is an identity.
questions.explanation: Addition can be neutral only at $0$, since $a+e=a$ gives $e=0$. But $0$ is excluded from the positive reals, so the restricted set has no identity.

questions.question: On a set $A$ with more than one element, define $a\star b=a$. Does this operation have a two-sided identity?
